topic.title: the drive back home
topic.claim: The first car isn't bought for your commute. It's bought for the drive back to your hometown.
topic.moment: You picture the new car and it's not the office parking lot, it's pulling up to your gate back home with your parents in it.

turn.believed: You bought the car to make the daily commute easier.
turn.actually: You bought it for the one journey that proves you made it: arriving home, at the wheel, with your parents in the back.

topic.because: The commute is just the reason you tell yourself. The real picture is the lane you grew up in, the neighbours watching, your parents sitting in the car their child bought. The car is a status you can drive to their doorstep.
topic.payoff: You didn't buy the car for the traffic. You bought it for the one drive where everyone back home sees who you've become.
topic.feeling: the quiet pride of coming home at the wheel
topic.villain: the arrangement that measures arrival by what you drive up in
topic.behaviour: people buy a first car and plan the big hometown roadtrip before anything else
topic.mechanism: the commute is the excuse, but the car's real job is to carry your parents home and show the lane you made it
topic.group: first-time car buyers from smaller towns
topic.send_to: a friend who just bought their first car and planned the hometown trip first
topic.why_now: festive-season car purchases and the holiday drive home

cover.headline: In India, a first car isn't bought by a person. [It's bought by a family.]
cover.sub: And everyone at home waited for it longer than you did.

paragraphs: In India, a first car isn't bought by a person. It's bought by a family.
Remember the day it came home.
Mummy at the door with a thali. Lemon and chillies on the bumper before it moved an inch. The first drive is to the temple, not the highway.
And papa. Twenty years on the same scooter. Now he walks around the car twice, touches the bonnet, and doesn't say much.
Anyone who has sold anything in India knows the buyer is rarely the real customer.
Your name is on the loan. The car was bought for the people who waited for it.
It goes back to the city, sits in traffic, and spends most of the week in a basement slot. Five years of EMIs for a car the family sees twice a year.
And I don't think that's silly.
For years your parents answered "beta kya karta hai" with a job title nobody back home could picture. The car at the gate, in the lane you grew up in, is the first answer they can point at.
**The EMI is in your name. The car was always in theirs.**

claims.text: Because families emotionally invest in and anticipate a first car's arrival, and because the loan is held individually while the car is intended to serve and represent the whole family, the first car purchase in India is effectively a family purchase rather than an individual one, even though only one person's name is on the loan.
claims.sentence: In India, a first car isn't bought by a person. It's bought by a family. ... Your name is on the loan. The car was bought for the people who waited for it.

a852887db2029aa46fec722ebc07eb4722fd5d11.actual_mechanism: In India a car loan is a contract between the lender and the named borrower(s): the EMI obligation sits with whoever signs, and a co-applicant is optional (and for most retail buyers the loan and the RC are in the single buyer's name). The most common tenure is 60 months (5 years), so 'five years of EMIs in your name' is factually standard. None of this contradicts the car being chosen for, used by, or symbolically belonging to the family — legal/financial liability and emotional/functional ownership are simply different things, which is exactly the post's point.

sources.quote: Most lenders in India offer car loans between 1 and 7 years (12 to 84 months), with the RC endorsed by the bank and the endorsement cancelled on repayment of the loan.
5 years is the most common tenure for car loans in India; the EMI obligation rests with the named borrower on the loan agreement.
